passage:
'Users dropped again,' Raghav said, turning the laptop around. 'Nine hundred, down from four thousand.'

'It's a dip,' said Hansa.

'Hansa, it's been two years of dips.'

'I put my savings in. The whole team's time. Two years. If we stop, all of it is gone.'

'And if you carry on?'

'Then we can fix it.'

'Fix what? Last month you told me you don't know why they leave.'

Hansa looked at the wall. 'I can't be the person who quit after two years.'

'The two years are gone either way. What matters is what the next year buys.'

'I don't have an answer,' said Hansa quietly. 'I just can't press the button.'

qa.a: Nine hundred users remained, down from four thousand.
Hansa is afraid of being the person who quit after two years, and feels the past effort would be wasted.

qa.q: What could Hansa do instead of carrying on?
qa.a: Hansa could set a review point with clear numbers and find out why users leave, then decide by what the next year could bring, not by what was spent.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel during this talk?
qa.a: Raghav may feel worried and frustrated but caring, trying to help Hansa look ahead.

grounding: Shows a founder continuing a failing product for two years because of what has already been invested.

subtype: Approach: keeps going only because so much has been invested [Pitfall]
passage: Looking back, I can see exactly where I went wrong. I'm Vijay. My co-founder Omkar and I built a meal-kit service in our early twenties. In the first year, customers came. In the second, they left. Every month the numbers dropped, and every month I said, "We've put in too much to stop now. Two years, our savings, my father's loan." Omkar once asked, "If we were starting today, would we choose this?" I got angry. I didn't want to hear it. We cut prices, tried new boxes, hired a marketer. Nothing brought customers back, and nobody could say how it would. We finally shut down owing more than before. What kept me going wasn't a plan. It was not wanting all that effort to feel wasted.

qa.a: "If we were starting today, would we choose this?"

qa.q: Why did Vijay get angry at Omkar's question?
qa.a: Vijay felt defensive and afraid; admitting the truth would have meant feeling that all the effort was wasted.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Decisions were made on what was already spent; asking Omkar's question seriously, perhaps with an outside mentor, would focus on what lay ahead.

qa.q: How was Omkar affected by Vijay's choice?
qa.a: Omkar was likely frustrated and worried, seeing the problem clearly but being shut down when raising it.

grounding: A founder keeps a failing product going for two years because of money and effort already spent, with no path to recovery.

passage:
Incubator mentor's note: Sumit and Sunaina, quarterly review

This is the eighth quarter I've reviewed their tutoring app. Active users are down for the fifth quarter in a row. The two schools that piloted it have left. When I asked Sumit what would make things turn around, he talked for ten minutes about how much they had built, the two years, the savings they had both put in, the features "almost ready". He did not describe a single customer who wanted it now. Sunaina was quiet; afterwards she told me she has wanted to stop since last year but Sumit "can't let it go". I have suggested they meet me next week with one question answered honestly: knowing what they know now, would they start this today?

qa.q: How many quarters in a row have active users dropped?
qa.a: Down for the fifth quarter in a row.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's quietness suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She seems weary and conflicted, wanting to stop but hesitant to push against Sumit.

qa.q: How could the mentor's question help Sumit?
qa.a: It asks him to judge the future, not the past, so the two years and savings stop being the reason to continue.

qa.q: How is Sunaina affected by Sumit's refusal to stop?
qa.a: Sunaina keeps putting time into a product she has doubted for a year, which likely leaves her frustrated and stuck.

grounding: A mentor notes a founder continuing a failing product because of what has already been spent, though users have left.
